beats.intro: Chapter nine, lesson seven. Chemiosmosis, A T P synthase, and the A T P count. [[dam]]Picture a dam on a river. The water piles up behind the wall, and it has stored energy. [[gate]]Open a gate, and the water rushes through a turbine, and the turbine turns. [[map]]Here is our map of cellular respiration again. [[lit]]Today we light up the last stage, oxidative phosphorylation, where the cell does something very like this, inside the mitochondrion. [[push]]Let's zoom into the inner membrane.
beats.pump: [[chain]]In the last lesson, electrons fell down the electron transport chain, from carrier to carrier, and ended on oxygen. [[pump]]The chain does something else along the way. Complexes one, three, and four use the energy of the falling electrons to pump H plus, protons, out of the matrix, and into the intermembrane space. [[grad]]So protons crowd in the narrow space on one side, and few remain in the matrix. That is an H plus gradient, a store of energy, like the water behind the dam. [[wall]]The membrane is the wall. Protons cannot simply cross it. The only open door is a protein called A T P synthase.
beats.synthase: [[parts]]A T P synthase has four parts. The stator is anchored in the membrane, and it stays still. The rotor is a ring of subunits in the membrane, and it can spin. The internal rod is a stalk that turns with the rotor. And the catalytic knob sits at the top of the rod, on the matrix side. [[one]]Step one. Protons flow down their gradient into a channel in the stator. [[two]]Step two. They bind to sites in the rotor, and change the shape of each subunit, so the rotor spins. [[three]]Step three. Each proton makes one full turn, and leaves through a second channel into the matrix. [[four]]Step four. The spinning rotor turns the rod, while the stator holds the knob still. [[five]]And step five. The turning rod activates the catalytic sites in the knob, which make A T P from A D P and phosphate. [[turbine]]It really is a tiny turbine. Moving protons turn it, and the turning makes A T P.
beats.q1: Quick check. Which part of the synthase spins, and which part stays still?
beats.force: [[chemi]]This use of the energy stored in an H plus gradient to do cellular work is called chemiosmosis. [[pmf]]Because the gradient can do work, it is called a proton motive force. [[couple]]It is the link between two worlds. On one side, the redox reactions of the chain. On the other, the making of A T P. The gradient couples them. [[whole]]Put the two halves together and you have oxidative phosphorylation. Part one, the electron transport chain, makes the gradient. Part two, chemiosmosis, uses the gradient to make A T P. Neither half makes A T P alone. [[flow]]So the energy flows like this. Glucose gives its electrons to N A D H. The slide leaves out F A D H 2, but it joins in at complex two. N A D H feeds the electron transport chain. The chain builds the proton motive force. And the proton motive force makes A T P.
beats.count: [[tally]]Now let's count the A T P from one glucose. [[gly]]Glycolysis makes two A T P, by substrate level phosphorylation. [[cyc]]The citric acid cycle makes two more, one for each turn, again by substrate level phosphorylation. [[carriers]]But look at what else was made. Two N A D H in glycolysis, two more in pyruvate oxidation, six N A D H and two F A D H 2 in the cycle. All of them deliver electrons to the chain. [[ox]]And oxidative phosphorylation turns that into about twenty six or twenty eight A T P. [[sum]]Add them up. Two plus two plus twenty six is thirty. Two plus two plus twenty eight is thirty two. So about thirty or thirty two A T P per glucose. [[most]]Notice that almost all of it, about nine in ten, comes from oxidative phosphorylation.
beats.estimate: [[why]]Why twenty six or twenty eight, and why only about? [[shuttle]]The N A D H made in glycolysis sits in the cytosol, and it cannot cross into the mitochondrion. Electron shuttles span the membrane and carry its electrons in. Depending on the shuttle, they arrive as two N A D H, or as two F A D H 2. F A D H 2 enters lower in the chain, so it pumps fewer protons, and gives less A T P. [[loose]]There is more. The proton gradient is also used for other work, so not every proton goes to A T P synthase. And the number of protons per A T P is not a whole number. [[est]]So thirty or thirty two is an estimate, a maximum, not an exact count. Say about, never exactly.
beats.q2: Quick check. Which stage makes the most of the cell's energy currency?
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[s1]]The chain pumps protons into the intermembrane space, and builds a gradient, a proton motive force. [[s2]]The protons flow back through A T P synthase, which spins like a turbine, and the knob makes A T P. That is chemiosmosis. [[s3]]Together, the chain and chemiosmosis are oxidative phosphorylation, and one glucose gives about thirty or thirty two A T P. [[end]]Now try the practice.
